Let’s group the penguins by species and calculate the average body mass of each species.This time, instead of a histogram like the Python post, but you want the numbers in a table instead.

penguins_species_weight = penguins |> 
  group_by(species) |> 
  summarise(avg_body_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
penguins_species_weight

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   avg_body_mass
  <fct>             <dbl>
1 Adelie            3701.
2 Chinstrap         3733.
3 Gentoo            5076.


Description: Of the three penguin species observed, the Gentoos are by far the biggest birds and thus, the most satisfyingly huggable ones.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation day - our favourite classroom.


The first week has been a whirlwind of challenges and delights, but reflection is needed after failing to complete 3 labs and multiple worksheets. The instructors and TAs are fantastic, and my colleagues were bright and encouraging. However, staying late and grinding slowly did not work.
This week’s game plan: 1. Rule 1: Do all worksheets and all labs ASAP. 2. Rule 2: Changes for pre-lecture readings:

Math: Ask AI to explain the textbook simply if you struggle with the textbook for 10 minutes.
R: Watch Dr. Timbers’s videos first (not the textbook or required readings).
Platforms: Reading first does not help if you don’t understand 80% of it.
Python: Read through ahead of class. Watch a YouTube video ifneed be. Haven’t figured this class out.

It feels doom-y, but it’s definitely not gloomy. Instructors and students are the highlight of each day. Onwards.

Why data science
Despite the wide range of jobs, the same questions kept resurfacing: What insights can be extracted from these data the team collected? How can those insights be communicated persuasively? How can systems outlast the people who build them? And how can AI and automation make work faster and more accurate, freeing up time for deeper analysis?
After more than a decade of trying to learn on her own, Joyce decided to enrolled in UBC’s Master of Data Science program. She’s interested in statistics, modelling, and the process of turning messy data into something meaningful. And while the learning curve is steep, but she’s enjoying the challenge and has been continually impressed by her instructors and cohort.

Data: Palmer Penguins,
Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

You’re a scientist in Palmer Station and and you wonder which penguin species on average will give the best hugs. You like hugs from big birds, so you decided to find out which species on average, are the chunkiest penguin.
This is what the original database looks like on the station’s computer. It’s a large dataset – you’re working with the brightest scientists after all.

Let’s find how many species are around the station, and their average body masses (rounded). You want to sort the database from heaviest to lightest.

# Group by 'species', find the mean, and sort by chunkiest penguin
penguins_species = penguins.groupby(by="species").mean(numeric_only = True).round().sort_values(by = "body_mass_g", ascending = False)

Finally, remove all the other columns that are not species or mass.

# Remove excess columns
penguins_species = penguins_species.drop(["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", "year"], axis = 1)

Here are the results. The Gentoo penguins are probably the most satisfyingly huggable ones with an average body mass of 5.1 kg.

penguins_species.plot.bar(y="body_mass_g")







Figure 1: Body mass of penguins by species.
